title_en: After Voting No, What Choices Remained?
title_zh: 投下“不”以后，还有哪些选择？
deck_en: A referendum, a new loan and a pay-slip challenged in court. Consent matters; so do the conditions under which a country can refuse.
deck_zh: 一场公投、一份新贷款，还有一张被诉到法院的工资单。同意重要，能够怎样拒绝也重要。
search_labels: Greece Greek bailout referendum OXI ESM EFSF IMF ECB Koufaki ADEDY 希腊 希臘 公投 救助 欧债危机 歐債危機 库法基 庫法基 欧洲稳定机制 歐洲穩定機制
body_zh: 2015年7月5日，希腊公投的有效票中，61.31%选择了“不”。这个结果不含糊。含糊的是，几周之后读者看到新的救助谈判时，该怎样理解这个“不”。[1]
若只留下两张新闻标题，故事很容易写完：人民拒绝了，政府后来却接受了。可真实的困难，还在标题之间。拒绝了哪一份提案？留下什么承诺？不接受新的贷款，又会发生什么？这些问题不能替投票消音，也不能被投票替代。
公投题目针对的是三家机构在6月25日提交欧元集团的提案，由改革方案和债务可持续性初步分析两份文件组成。它不是一张直接询问是否退出欧元的选票，也不是对任何未来贷款的永久否决。[2]
把题目说准，是尊重这次投票的第一步，却不是最后一步。不能因为后来签的是另一份协议，就轻巧地回答：法律对象不同，所以民意并没有落空。一个国家所能作出的选择，远比纸面上允许填写的答案更复杂。
## 选票之外，还有正在流失的时间
投票之前，银行危机已经逼近。6月28日，欧洲央行决定把希腊银行紧急流动性援助的上限维持在26日的水平，没有随需求继续提高。这里不是把现有援助一笔勾销；维持上限与切断一切资金，不是一回事。[3]
在资金持续流出的背景下，希腊当局实施银行假日和资本管制。不能把关闭银行直接写成欧洲央行替希腊政府下的一道命令；也不能因为最后的法律动作出自本国，就说外部决定对实际余地没有影响。欧洲审计院后来梳理的时间线，把这些相互牵动的环节放在了一起。[4]
这使7月5日不再像一道考卷上的选择题。考卷允许你先把答案想明白，生活却还在往下走。银行能否支付、国家何时到期还债、谈判还能等多久，都在改变拒绝一项条件需要付出的代价。
欧盟此前的援助计划在6月30日到期。7月8日，希腊申请欧洲稳定机制的新贷款；8月19日，新计划启动。公投与新协议之间，确实有新的申请、谈判和批准程序，不是把投票所针对的两份文件改个封面就原样执行。[5]
但新程序的存在，还不能回答旧的不满到了哪里。一个人可以认为当时继续谈判是较少伤害的选择，同时追问：为什么可以谈的空间已经如此狭窄？被迫在坏处之间挑选，并不会因为最后有人签字，就变成对全部安排的满意。
另一边也有不能省略的人。其他国家的政府要向本国议会和公众解释，为什么动用资源继续贷款、由谁承受风险。希腊选民的“不”不能自动变成其他社会必须按原条件继续出钱的“是”。多国合作难就难在，没有哪一张选票能独自替所有人说完。
这不是把双方写成一样有力。形式上都需要同意，手里能等的时间、能承受的中断和握有的资源却可能差得很远。同意不是没有意义；只是不能把同意当作一句不用再查条件的结案词。
## 一张援助账，几种不同的钱
把镜头往前移，事情又多了一层。2010年的第一轮欧洲援助，主要通过欧元区国家的双边贷款机制，另有国际货币基金组织贷款；2012年的第二轮转到欧洲金融稳定工具等安排；2015年的第三轮才由欧洲稳定机制提供贷款。不能把八年里的出资方统称为一个从未改变的“救助机构”。[5]
机构名字不是为了让读者背缩写。重要的是：谁决定拨款，谁提出条件，谁执行国内措施，谁有权重看哪一部分。若全写成“欧洲要求”，责任就会大到无法落在任何一项决定上，也小到每个参与者都能说自己只负责其中一点。
第三轮计划的上限是八百六十亿欧元，实际由欧洲稳定机制拨出的贷款为六百一十九亿欧元，计划在2018年8月20日结束。上限与实拨要分开；贷款也不是一笔不必偿还、可以全部直接分给居民的赠款。[6]
一笔用于偿还到期债务的钱，可以防止支付链条在眼前断掉，却不会因此成为家庭账户里新增的同额收入。反过来，没有直接发给居民，也不证明资金对居民全无帮助。银行、政府支付与普通生活之间有联系，只是这种联系需要说明，不能由“救助”两个字包办。
“稳定”于是有了不同的距离。对贷款机构，可能是下一笔款项能否按时支付；对一份预算，是收支能否达到要求；对靠工资或养老金生活的人，则可能是调整以后还能怎样安排日子。它们并不天然冲突，也不天然重合。
更难的是，起初相信的复苏未必按时出现。国际货币基金组织2013年对第一轮方案的事后评估承认，实际衰退远深于原先预测，失业高于预期，并讨论了财政收缩的影响、改革推进、信心和其他因素。这是参与机构回头审视自己的判断，不是一份宣布所有损失只有一个原因的判决。[7]
预测失准不是一项可以悄悄修掉的笔误。若人们接受眼前削减，是因为相信几年后能够恢复，那么恢复推迟，就改变了这份安排原先要求他们相信的东西。原来的理由还算不算数，需要再说，不能只把新数字填进旧承诺。
当然，重新计算也不能许诺一种没有代价的替代历史。更早重组债务、慢一点调整、采取不同税制，各有需要证明的效果与风险。“另有选择”应当把选择讲得更具体，而不是给事后的我们发一张永远不会出错的通行证。
## 工资单进入法院以后
在这些宏观数字旁边，有一份可以回查的个人请求。库法基对本人的工资削减提出挑战，公务员工会联合会ADEDY也质疑紧缩措施。2013年5月7日，欧洲人权法院在库法基与ADEDY诉希腊案中，认定有关申诉明显缺乏根据，不予受理。[8]
这里的法院不是负责发放贷款的欧洲稳定机制，也不是欧盟法院。它审查的是特定措施在《欧洲人权公约》财产权保护下的问题。不能把这项决定改写成欧洲各机构一起宣布：八年救助的全部经济政策都是最佳方案。
法院考虑了严重危机、立法机关在社会经济政策上的裁量空间，以及申诉人所承受的负担。它没有承担替希腊选择最佳预算的任务。申诉没有成功，却让“居民承担代价”不再只是一句由作者代说的话：至少在这个案子里，有具体的人把一项措施变成了需要回答的法律问题。[8]
这也提醒我们，不能笼统地说个人没有任何救济途径。有途径，与这条途径能够审查整个谈判、改变拨款时点、重订国家预算，是不同的事。一次法律请求的边界，不等于一个人的全部问题已经被穷尽。
有人可能完全遵守了程序，仍然无法回答另一个问题：如果调整持续得比预想更久，那些最难承受的人，还能通过什么办法让自己的处境进入下一轮决定？法院、议会、谈判和公共讨论各有位置，没有哪一个可以轻易包下其余几个。
而援助确实做过的工作，也不必为了保留这个问题而被删除。贷款提供了实际资金，第三轮计划最终结束。结束一个计划是一项可以确认的事实；它不等于每个家庭都恢复到危机前，也不等于以后的债务与监督从此不存在。[5][6]
希腊这段历史最不适合被压成一句关于服从或任性的寓言。它里面既有必须共同承担的金融风险，也有不断移动的预测；既有国家作出的承诺，也有个人没有亲自签下、却必须生活在其中的后果。
公投的重要，不在于它能用一声“不”立即改变所有外部条件。它让拒绝留下一个清楚的记录。但记录之后还有工作：解释后来为什么接受，哪些要求仍在争取，哪些伤害不能因为资金到账就不再提。
如果共同决定值得保留，也许正因为它应当让人获得比独自面对危机更多的余地。而要知道它是否做到了，不能只看协议有没有签、程序有没有走完，还得看拒绝之后留下了什么选择，接受之后还能不能再问。
61.31%的有效票选择了“不”。下一份协议后来签下了。这两句话都是真的。把它们之间那段艰难的路写出来，才是这段历史还值得重读的地方。
body_en: On 5 July 2015, 61.31% of valid votes in Greece’s referendum were cast for No. The number is clear. What becomes much less clear, looking at the assistance agreement reached later that summer, is what the refusal was able to change.[1]

Two headlines can turn this into a very short story: the public rejected the terms; the government subsequently accepted a bailout. But the distance between those headlines contains the difficult questions. Which proposal was rejected? What was still open to negotiation? What would refusing the next agreement have meant?

The ballot concerned a proposal presented to the Eurogroup on 25 June, comprising a reform document and a preliminary debt-sustainability analysis. It was not a direct vote on leaving the euro, nor a permanent rejection of every possible future assistance package.[2]

Accuracy about that question is necessary. It is not sufficient. Saying that the eventual agreement was legally different cannot by itself settle what happened to the political refusal. A country may retain the formal power to decline an offer while finding the range of survivable alternatives painfully narrow.
## The calendar outside the polling station

Before the vote, banking pressure was already acute. On 28 June, the European Central Bank maintained the ceiling on emergency liquidity assistance to Greek banks at its 26 June level. Holding a ceiling unchanged was not the same as withdrawing all existing assistance. It was also not an assurance that assistance would expand to meet further outflows.[3]

Against the background of deposit withdrawals, the Greek authorities imposed a bank holiday and capital controls. Those were domestic measures, not simply an ECB order closing Greek banks. Yet locating the formal domestic decision does not remove the surrounding constraints. The European Court of Auditors’ later chronology records how these developments interacted.[4]

A ballot does not stop that calendar. Debts mature, payment systems need liquidity and negotiations consume time. These are not reasons to disregard a vote. They are reasons why saying No in a crisis can mean something very different from selecting No on a form with no consequences until the answers have been collected.

The previous European programme expired on 30 June. Greece requested a new ESM loan on 8 July; the new programme began on 19 August. There was a new request, negotiation and approval process, not merely the implementation under a new cover of the two documents on the referendum ballot.[5]

Nevertheless, procedure does not make the disappointment disappear. One can judge continued negotiation to have been the less damaging course and still ask why the space for negotiation had become so limited. Acceptance under severe pressure is a decision. It is not necessarily satisfaction with the conditions, and it cannot retrospectively turn a refusal into enthusiasm.

Other societies were implicated too. Governments providing assistance had to answer to their own publics and legislatures about resources and risk. A Greek No could not automatically become an obligation on everyone else to continue lending on unchanged terms. No single national electorate could give the last answer for all the participants.

That observation does not make their bargaining positions equal. The ability to wait, endure an interruption or find another source of finance can differ enormously. Consent still matters in such a situation. What it cannot do is end the inquiry into the circumstances under which it was obtained. A signature records a decision; it does not measure the freedom of every alternative.
## Money is not one thing

Looking back to 2010 reveals another reason to avoid a single undifferentiated villain or rescuer. The first European package used bilateral euro-area lending through the Greek Loan Facility, alongside IMF lending. The second involved the EFSF; the third, in 2015, used the ESM. It was not one unchanged institution operating for eight years.[5]

The acronyms matter only because powers and responsibilities matter. Who can release a tranche? Who proposes a condition? Who legislates it at home? Who can reconsider it? Calling every decision ‘Europe’s demand’ can make responsibility simultaneously immense and elusive: everyone participates, yet each actor appears responsible only for a fragment.

The third programme had a maximum envelope of €86 billion. The ESM actually disbursed €61.9 billion before the programme ended on 20 August 2018. A ceiling is not a disbursement. These were loans, not a grant whose entire face value could simply be divided among households.[6]

Money used to meet a maturing debt can prevent an immediate break in payments without appearing as an equivalent increase in family income. Conversely, the absence of a direct household transfer does not establish that the financing provided no household benefit. The connection between sovereign payments, banks and ordinary life needs explaining, rather than being settled by the word ‘rescue’.

Stability can consequently refer to different distances from the same event. For a financing institution, it may concern the next payment. For a budget, it may concern the required balance. For someone living on wages or a pension, the question is how life can be arranged after an adjustment. These perspectives can support one another. They need not coincide automatically.

Nor did recovery arrive as originally expected. The IMF’s 2013 evaluation of the first programme acknowledged a downturn much deeper than projected and unemployment above expectations. It examined fiscal contraction, implementation, confidence and other factors. This was a participant’s retrospective evaluation, not a finding that all losses had a single cause.[7]

A failed forecast is more than a number to correct quietly in the next document. If immediate sacrifices were justified partly by an expected recovery, a delayed recovery changes the proposition people were asked to accept. The reasons must be explained again. An updated spreadsheet cannot do that work on its own.

There is no costless alternative history waiting to be inserted here. Earlier restructuring, slower adjustment or a different tax mix each requires evidence about effects and risks. Asking whether another course was possible should make alternatives more specific. It should not give hindsight the privilege of proposing choices that never have to encounter the world.
## A pay-slip becomes a legal question

Alongside the aggregate figures there is a documented individual challenge. Ioanna Koufaki contested her pay reduction; the public-service union confederation ADEDY also challenged austerity measures. On 7 May 2013, the European Court of Human Rights declared the relevant complaints inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded.[8]

This court was neither the ESM lender nor the European Union’s Court of Justice. It addressed particular measures under the Convention’s property protection. Its decision cannot be expanded into a collective institutional declaration that every economic policy adopted across eight years was either lawful in every respect or the best available policy.

The court considered the exceptional crisis, the legislature’s latitude in social and economic policy and the burden on the applicants. It did not undertake to choose the best national budget. The application failed, but the record still matters: a specific person had made a specific reduction a question requiring a legal answer, rather than remaining merely an example in someone else’s account of public hardship.[8]

It would therefore be inaccurate to say that individuals had no remedy of any kind. Having a route to challenge a pay measure is nevertheless different from being able to reopen the entire assistance negotiation or alter a disbursement date. The reach of a legal proceeding cannot tell us that a person’s whole difficulty has been heard.

A further question survives even meticulous procedure. If adjustment lasts longer than anticipated, how can those least able to bear it bring that fact into the next decision? Courts, parliaments, negotiations and public argument do different work. None should be expected to replace all the others merely because it has delivered an answer within its own remit.

Keeping that question open does not require deleting what assistance did provide. Loans supplied real financing; the third programme eventually ended. Programme completion is a verifiable institutional event. It is not evidence that every household had recovered, or that debt and oversight ceased to matter afterwards.[5][6]

The Greek case resists being made into a fable about either obedience or irresponsibility. Shared financial risks were real. So were revisable forecasts and uneven burdens. Governments made commitments, while individuals had to live with consequences they had not personally negotiated. Understanding that combination takes more work than identifying which side signed last.

The referendum’s significance was not that a No could immediately alter every external condition. It made refusal unmistakably part of the record. What followed still required an account: why an agreement was accepted, what remained contested, and which costs could not be declared irrelevant simply because finance had arrived.

Perhaps the most persuasive reason for a shared arrangement is that it should offer more room than confronting a crisis alone. Whether it did so cannot be judged only by a signed agreement or a completed procedure. We also need to ask what alternatives remained after refusal, and what questions could still be raised after acceptance.

Most valid votes said No. Another agreement was subsequently signed. Both statements are true. The difficult road between them is not an embarrassing interval to hurry past. It is the part of the history we most need to read.
